speechtext: LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 88) respecting assaults and offences against the person.

maintopic: ASSAULTS AND OFFENCES AGAINST THE PERSON.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: ASSAULTS AND OFFENCES AGAINST THE PERSON.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill has reference to crimes that now, unfortunately, are too prevalent throughout the whole of Canada. There is no one within sound of my voice but will admit that there has been a strange laxity in the punishment of offenders against the person while those frequently found pilfering a small sum of money with which to purchase something to eat are punished too severely. The purpose of the Bill is to increase the punishment of tramps or others who commit offences against the person and to take proper care of persons dangerous to be at large. We must recollect that twenty years have elapsed since the Criminal Code was first made law in this country. Times have changed, our circumstances have altered and our population has increased. Throughout this fair Canada of ours crimes against the person of a very objectionable character are rampant. The murderer, the burglar, ravisher, the assaulter, gets off with a small punishment. Unfortunately there is a practice prevailing which is not calculated to mitigate this condition. A tramp who is arrested in a certain county is allowed his liberty by the magistrate on condition that he goes into another county within so many hours.
In the recent Stratford case, where the negro broke into the house and murdered a woman after assaulting her, the negro had been arrested three times within one week before the murder, but had been allowed to go by different magistrates on condition that he removed into another county. The seventh clause of this Bill prohibits a magistrate from allowing a criminal, a vagrant, an idle or a dissolute person to go free on condition that he leaves the county. It also provides that where a vagrant, an idle or a dissolute person has been convicted a second time he shall be sent to a prison or penitentiary provided by the province in which he is charged, there to be detained at hard labour until the inspector certifies that from his course in the penitentiary or from his having learned a trade there, he is, in the opinion of the inspector, able and willing to earn an honest living and not be a menace to -his fellows. Where a prisoner, after being liberated, in that way, commits another offence, then in addition to the punishment for that offence, he shall be sentenced to from five to ten years in the penitentiary. Tallack, on the Law of Crime, distinctly lays down that the first act of violence predisposes to a criminal disposition, and that where a person has 1 Mr. SPEAKER.
been convicted three times he should be treated as incorrigible and kept where he will not be a menace to his fellow men. Clause 6 authorizes the nolice to search tramps, idle and dissolute persons for weapons and prescribe punishments
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 89) to amend the Government Harbours and Piers Act.
He said:	The object of this Bill is to
provide for the leasing of breakwaters, wharfs and piers which are under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, to municipal corporations or railways or shipping companies. The existing law provides that municipal corporations may become the lessees of wharfs. There is no provision as far as shipping companies and railway companies are concerned, and it has been thought advisable that they should have the power to lease wharfs. As a matter of fact such a power exists before the wharfs and piers and transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. There is a provision in the Public Works Act declaring that these wharfs and piers may be leased to shipping and railway companies and to municipal corporations. The present Bill is simply an extension of this power granted under the Public Works Act to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
The second clause provides for the commuting of wharfage rates. The collection of the small wharfage fees on some of these . minor wharfs becomes a very serious difficulty for the department. We think that if we had the power to commute the fees with the shipping companies it would give us a larger revenue than we now receive.
Motion agreed to, and the Bill read the first time.

['This Bill is a very considerable change from the provisions of the law which hitherto have governed our immigration system, and I have no hesitation in saying that it is a step forward upon the lines which have very often been advocated in this House, and more particularly on this side of the House. As I understand the measure, it does not in any way interfere with the system of favouring immigration which has existed hitherto; it does not disturb in any manner our immigration agencies established in the United States, in the British Isles and on the continent. It in no way changes the system of bonusing immigrants which has hitherto existed, and in', "relation to which we are still governed by the order in council which has considerably enlarged the system, extending it to railway navvies and other classes, which, up to the time of passing that order in council, never had been comprised within the bonus system. What the Bill aims at particularly is to provide for a strict examination of immigrants when they land in Canada. It has been found-there is no doubt whatever about it-that our system of examination was utterly deficient. And the object of this legislation is to provide a system that will assure a more careful examination of incoming immigrants. I say that, so far as that goes, this law is a step forward. But the question which suggests itself, I am sure, to every member of this House who has taken any interest in the question of immigration is this: If this is a good law, if it provides a safeguard, against a class of immigrants who are not desirable in this country, whv has it not been enacted sooner? While giving credit to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) for this measure, I say it is fit and proper for us to ask why this safeguard was not provided ten or twelve years ago when we began receiving in this country such large quantities of immigration, when from an expenditure of about $100,000 a year or $125,000 a year, which was our limit up to 1896, we went up to an expenditure of $700,000, $800,000, and finally, even more than $1,000,000. As a consequence of a very much more expensive propaganda and the establishment of far more numerous agencies and of a system of bonusing which had never been known before, we have had an immense influx of immigrants. The conditions prescribed by this Bill were known to be necessary at that time. They were urged on this side of the House repeatedly when that wave of immigration began to invade Canada. This measure is taken largely from the American immigration regulations and law. Why did not we adopt it before? That is the serious observation I wish to lay before the minister-let him tell us why we are, so to speak, locking the stable door after the horse is gone? For that is what we are doing. The explanation must certainly be found in the fact that, during a certain number of years which former members of this House will certainly remember, we had given to the tendency of immigration to this country a push forward which was extremely imprudent. Not to go too extensively into affairs of the past, it will be remembered that, through the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company largely, the country paid out, speaking off-hand, but I think pretty closely to the figures-over $450,000 in bonuses and expenses of advertising. It will hardly be denied that in this we were doing an extremely imprudent Mr. MONK.
thing, for we never were able to find out what became of that money and to whom it was paid. I do not wish to go at too great a length into that phase of the question, and to recall a past which most of those who took an interest in the question at that time, I am sure, have still in mind. This proposed legislation, to my mind, shows the usefulness of the campaign, in this House and outside of this House, which was kept up by the opposition for a long time in order to secure the very provisions that we find in this Bill. And it is extremely regretable, I am sure, not only in the interests of our country, but in the interests of the immigrants of the better class who have come here and succeeded, that these enactments were not put into law before the large influx of immigrants into Canada, amounting, I suppose, in the last ten years, to over 800,000 people, had begun.
Let me say a word with regard to one of the dispositions of the Bill, and which is continued, if I may say so, in the principle of the Bill. The whole Bill proceeds upon what is to my mind a bad principle, and I venture to say that before long we will come to the conclusion in this House and in the country that that principle is not well founded. The whole Bill is founded on the principle of the examination of the immigrant after he lands, or is about to land, in Canada. I think that experience has demonstrated, and statistics will show, that this is a wrong principle. We should make sure that the immigrant is a fit and proper person to come to this country before he leaves the port of embarkation. This is what happens in practice: The immigrant will go to the booking agent, we will say, in the British Isles or on the continent. The agent is anxious in the first place to bring this immigrant within the bonus class, and I submit to my hon. friend the minister that with the wide order in council authorizing the payment of bonuses, it is not a very difficult task for an experienced booking agent to get that immigrant into the class which earns him a bonus. No examination whatever as to the physical condition of the immigrant takes place before landing. There is no inquiry whatever as to his moral qualifications to become a citizen of this Dominion. All that takes place is that the booking agent makes sure that he will earn, through this immigrant, his. bonus, and sells him a ticket. Everything induces the agent to direct this immigrant to Canada, if possible, not only because of the bonus he receives, but because of the generous commission he gets from the transportation company.
The immigrant arrives in Quebec, we will say. Now members of this House who have followed the proceedings of the Immigration Committee in the past sessions, know what

kind of an examination the immigrant undergoes there. It is exceedingly brief.- I think it was Mr. Scott, the superintendent, who told us that the examination is a matter of two or three minutes, or perhaps four minutes. The immigrant passes before a medical examiner at the port of arrival. There are a thousand or two thousand immigrants to be examined, and a train is waiting to carry them on to their destination. He will look at their eyes, at their external appearance, but no proper medical examination takes place. And I ask the House how is it possible in the short space allowed to the examiner, to make sure, even in the most superficial manner, of the qualifications of the immigrant to enter this country. He passes before a second officer and is immediately hastened on board the train, and moves away. Now what happens ? He arrives in Montreal or Toronto. The man we will suppose, is undesirable; we will suppose that he is guilty of some offence. He is immediately brought before one of our criminal courts, either for some worse or some petty offence. The magistrate asks him where he comes from, what steamship line brought him across. He is remanded, and through the immigration agent, as I understand, the department of my hon. friend the minister is communicated with. The department sends an officer to make sure of the fact. Deportation in that case is found necessary; the man is at our expense detained in jail, he is afterwards forwarded with a guardian at the expense of the country, as a rule, to the port where he landed, for instance at Quebec. When the steamer is out in the stream ready to go, he is taken on board the vessel and sent home. He arrives in Liverpool. They don't want him there, and will not receive him. He is sent on perhaps to London, and there what is the condition of that man ? It may be that he is only in the early stage of criminality, but he is an absolutely lost individual, utterly discouraged, ostracized, and his fate is one, although he may be a criminal, very much to be deplored.
In the case of those who are deported because they are afflicted with disease, which very often happens-we had last year over 800 deported after admission to this country-the case is infinitely more pitiful. The man is returned to the company that has brought him over, and he is sent back. If
he is the father of a family who came out here to prospect and found an establishment, he returns to his home in Europe, having expended all the money he had when he came out here to establish a home. He is absolutely discouraged, and becomes a very active agent in doing as much harm as possible to this country, spreading everywhere the idea that this is the very worst country a man could come to. Very often families are separated, and the utmost distress and grief accompany this deportation. Cases have come under my observation where the hardship is very great indeed. I have known of other cases of people deported from Montreal who, after having done a great deal of harm in that city, in a variety of ways which it is not necessary to dilate upon now, have been sent back to their own country. There was a case came under my own personal knowledge of a prostitute who arrived in this country from Europe. There was nothing apparently to prevent her admission to this country. She came to Montreal and established a house there, and after a time was brought before the magistrate, and had to be deported. It is evident that it was impossible at the port of entry to discover the objection that existed in that case, and a great deal of harm resulted. There is no doubt whatever that if inquiries had been made, and if that person had been told on the other side that it was absolutely useless for her to attempt to enter Canada, we would have been spared the expense and the disagreeable consequences which resulted in that case.
I have a few more remarks to make on this subject, but as we have now passed the hour of six o'clock I move that the debate be adjourned."]

MURPHY (Secretary of State) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient that there should he a department of the civil service of Canada to be called the Department of External Affairs, over which the Secretary of State of Canada shall preside, and that the Governor in Council may appoint an officer to be the deputy head of such department at a salary of $5,000 per annum, and such other officers and olerks as may be requisite for the due administration of such department at such salaries as, under the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, are appropriate to the divisions and subdivisions of the service to which such officers and clerks may be assigned.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I desire to say
that the Bill to be founded on this resolution does not involve any serious constitutional change. It aims merely at an improvement in the administration of that class of public affairs which relate to matters other than those of purely internal concern. As the House is aware the Government of Canada holds all its official communications extending beyond the bounds of the Dominion, whether with the Secretary of State for the Colonies, with the various sister dominions, or with His Majesty's

ambassadors to foreign countries, through His Excellency the Governor General; and I might say for the information of the House that it is not proposed to effect any change in this regard by the legislation that is now proposed.
The House is also, I take it, aware, that despatches bearing on all questions of an external character come through His Excellency the Governor General. They are by His Excellency referred to the Privy Council and by the Privy Council they are in turn referred to the particular department which is supposed to be specially concerned with the subject matter of the communication. In due course the minister at the head of that department reports on these despatches to the Governor General in Council and that report, if agreed to by council and approved by His Excellency, is transmitted as the answer of his government. Now, this plan looks simple and in the early days of the Dominion it may have worked satisfactorily. These days however are passed, and with the development of the country and the increase in the number and complexity of its international relations it is felt that the old system is inadequate to meet the existing requirements. Those members of the House who are also members of the Privy Council know that official correspondence does not always lend itself to the simple treatment I have outlined. Sometimes it is difficult to tell at first sight to what department a despatch may relate; sometimes a despatch may relate partly to one department and partly to another or to several departments ; and it frequently happens that where despatches of a series are referred to a particular department others of the same series may later on find their way to another department which having no knowledge of the earlier correspondence will be at a loss to decide what shall be done. The government feel that it would be a great advantage if all such communications were sent to a common centre where they could be dealt with according to a uniform system; where there would be a small staff of officials trained in the study of these questions, and where at all times it would be possible to ascertain not only the present position of a question but its history from the very beginning. It is with the object of attaining these results that the present resolution is submitted to the House and that the Bill to be founded upon it later will be introduced.

The Secretary of State has not made one thing manifest to my mind, and that is the most important thing of all:	Why is it that the Department of the Secretary of State cannot be the common centre to which the hon. gentleman alludes; why cannot that department do all

the work that has been outlined in the very brief remarks of the Secretary of State ?
Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER
(Prime Minister). The Secretary of State has I think given the reasons why it is deemed advisable at this stage of our national development to have a department of external affairs. All governments have found it necessary to have a department whose only business shall be to deal with relations with foreign countries, and in our judgment Canada has reached a period in her history when we should follow the example of other countries in that respect, as, for example, the Commonwealth of Australia. In the Department of the Interior we have a department which deals with interior affairs and we have also a department which deals with Indian Affairs alone, it having been found long ago that the dealings with our aborigines required the attention of one department. So it is in the Department of Marine and Fisheries where we have practically one department dealing with marine affairs and another dealing with questions appertaining to our fisheries. I suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. R.
L.	Borden) that we have now reached a standard as a nation which necessitates the establishment of a Department of External Affairs. It is not unnatural that the hon. gentleman should ask, why the machinery of the Department of the Secretary of State is not sufficient for the purpose. We have given this matter a good deal of consideration and the conclusion we have_ arrived at is that the foreign affairs with which Canada has to deal are becoming of such absorbing moment as to necessitate special machinery. Look at the volume of business of an external character which has been transacted during the past year. We had the French treaty negotiated by us, of course with the concurrence and approval of the imperial authorities; we had another treaty dealing with the long pending question of the interpretation of the treaty of 1818 in relation to our Atlantic fisheries. For the last forty or fifty years this has been a source of contention between the United States and Great Britain although luckily during the last ten or twelve years we have had no serious difficulty with our neighbours in regard to it. However, our fellow subjects in Newfoundland have not been so fortunate and as we know they have had during the last four or five years some very acute differences with the American authorities on the subject of the interpretation of the treaty of 1818.	.
And, as a consequence, an arbitration has been determined upon to settle the points of difference between Newfoundland and the American authorities. We have been drawn into this contest; we have gone into it, not because we had any controver-

sy of our own, but simply because our fellow-subjects in Newfoundland were in it, an<^+i!'re bought it our duty to give them all the assistance we could in their difficulty. then, we have had another treatv. also negotiated at Washington, with reference to the fisheries in the inland waters. We have another treaty to mark again the boundaries between Canada and the United btates,-not to create any new boundary, but simply to place new land marks to show plainly where the boundary is. Then, wehave had another and most important treaty which is now engaging the attention of the American Senate, which, I hope, will come before the Canadian parliament before many days are over, that is, a treaty to in a friendly spirit all difficulties which may arise in the boundary waters between Canada and the United States. Then, the House is aware that, from time to time, we have had informal negotiations with Germany in relation to the tariff difficulty we have had with that country. Now-this alone will show to the House that Canada has reached a position where foreign relations have assumed a very important character. That is not surprising. We have now a population which cannot be less than six millions and is probably more; we have an annual revenue of $80,000,000 and more; our trade last year grew to the very large figure of $600,000,000. Under such circumstances, I repeat, it is not extraordinary that the volume of foreign affairs has assumed such proportions as to make it indispensable that we should have officers, trained for the purpose, whose business shall be to deal with such questions and such questions alone. Let me call the attention of the House to the character of the communications we received and whicji are to be classed as belonging to foreign relations. All our communications pass through the colonial office or the ambassador of His Majesty at Washington or elsewhere, and then come to the Governor General. From the Governor General, they are sent to the Privy Council-
The Secretary of State is it not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, to the Privy Council. It is not our intention to disturb that. It is better that the representative of the Sovereign should receive all communications relating to foreign affairs, and it is natural that by him they should be sent to the Privy Council. At present, from the Privy Council, they are sent to the department to which they relate.
How is that distribution made? Through the Secretary of State?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, by the Privy Council itself. All the despatches are sent from the Governor General to the
Privy Council; the clerk of the Privy Council places them before the council, and by the council they are assigned to the department to which they relate. But this is done sometimes in a hurry, and therefore it happens that despatches may go to the wrong department. For, my hon. friend will understand, ministers sitting at the council board have not the time to look into these matters themselves, and must depend upon their officers. The intention is that we should have a department which will be a department of Foreign Affairs and will deal with nothing else. All the despatches will be sent by the Privy Council to that department.
They will come first to the Governor General, then to the Privy Council, then to the department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, the Department of External Affairs. There they are docketed, they are digested and prepared.

How prepared?
Sir WILFR1D LAURIER. A memorandum is made-that is how I would work it out.
They would be abstracted-a precis made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Very good they would be abstracted, then sent to the proper department for information. The Department of External Affairs would receive this information, digest it and draft an answer to be sent to the minister and by him submitted to the council for its action.

I would like to ask one question. Will this department take up despatches, let us say, relating to a fisheries question, and prepare an answer to them and submit it to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. Suppose that a despatch relating to some foreign affair comes to the Privy Council-suppose that it relates to this very fisheries question, of which I spoke a moment ago-the Atlantic fisheries. That despatch will go to the Department of External Affairs. I vvould like to have a history of every question made, and kept up from day to day, so that the minister in charge, might, in a moment, understand what the question is and be prepared to advise the Governor General as to the policy that ought to be followed. If it is necessary to get information from the Department of Marine and Fisheries, it will go to fhat department. The Department of External Affairs will thus get all the technical details upon which to base a conclusion. It will also prepare a memorandum or draft of despatch, or answer, to be laid before council, on which a

policy can be adopted. Take, for instance, a question that was familiar to my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) when he was in office- the question of the seal fisheries of the Pacific ocean. This is a most complicated question, one which comes to the front from time to time and may come up again. Suppose we receive from the British Ambassador a despatch on this question. This despatch will be referred to the Department of External Affairs. All the information upon the question is collected, so that we can deal intelligently with the proposition which may be made to us. It may be, it will be sent to the Marine and Fisheries Department to get the information needed to deal with it. And when the matter is in proper shape, the Department of External Affairs will prepare a memorandum for the minister.
Which minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Secretary of State, the head of the department. He will bring it before council and by council the matter will be dealt with. This is the only reasonable way in which we can deal with these matters. At present, these questions are carried to different departments, there is no department in which we can collect a history of the several questions, and no officers trained to give us the advice we need in order to deal with these questions. When I was in England some years ago, I took pains to learn how these things were dealt with there. I found that in the Colonial office and in the Foreign office there are officers especially trained to keep up all the information needed to deal with the questions that may arise, keeping up the history of each question from day to day, so that, in a moment, the ministers may know where they are. I may be asked-I take it that such is the effect of the question asked by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden): Why not have this done by the Secretary of State's department? Why have another department? I have simply to answer that, in such experience of the government, as I have had leads me to believe that we have attained such development as a nation that in order to deal with these matters, we must have a department for the purpose. It is not intended it shall be a very numerous department, a very heavy department; I think the officers at present in the service can do the necessary work. But I think it is essential that we should have this department by itself, with nothing else to do but to give their special attention, and all their attention, to these matters alone.

I have been listening to the Prime Minister for information. What I want to get at, if possible, is the modus operandi which it is proposed to employ, and something of the extent and cost which that modus operandi will involve. From Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the remarks made by the Secretary of State, who did not go into it very extensively, I could not get into my mind just the method which it was proposed to proceed upon to accomplish the object. The Prime Minister has gone more into detail, and he has opened up what appears to him to be the method which should be pursued. Now, no one is more happy than myself, than the members on this side of the House, in common with every other citizen of Canada, at what may be the indication of Canada's extending business, not only internally, but with foreign countries, with the sister colonies, and with Great Britain. But the Prime Minister must not try to make us believe that there never were any external relations of importance until within these last few years. _ Canada has seldom been without her outside vexing questions, that have been from time to time of greater or less importance. It is not necessary to mention them, they come to the mind of every person who has had 25 or 30 years experience in public matters in this country. We have such questions now, we always will have them, and it is natural to suppose that they will be more extended in proportion as we grow, and the means of communication with the world becomes more rapid.
Now let us see what my hon. friend proposes, and inquire whether his idea will work out or not. It is not proposed to make any constitutional change; we are thankful for that. The despatch, when it enters Canada, will go to the Governor General as at the present time; the Governor General will then put that despatch into the possession of the Privy Council as quickly as possible, doing that because the head of the Privy Council is the premier of the country, who should first have notice of these despatches. They go to the Privy Council under the present and the past method of action. It has been the duty of the Privy Council to send these particular despatches each to the Minister of the department which was concerned. It is not a difficult matter surely for the ministers around _ the table in the Privy Council almost immediately to decide as to whether such and such a despatch affects the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or affects the Department of Agriculture or affects any other department. It shows on its face the subject matter, and the moment subject matter is shown, it goes by consequence to the minister in charge of the department in which those matters are carried on. It may take a little time, it may call for a little discernment, but I do not think the difficulties in that respect are at all large. Under the proposed plan, the Prime Minister will be rid of all' that difficulty, of having any initial discussion or investigation with regard to despatches that come in, by immediately bundling

them off to the Secretary of State. There may be an advantage in that in one way, there may be a disadvantage in another. It is an advantage that every member of the Council should have a constant and current knowledge of whatever is coming in from external sources affecting the business of Canada, that it should enter the Privy Council, and after it has passed through this process of digestion, come again before the Privy Council for ultimate decision. It may be some disadvantage that the matters which will receive the least consideration first will be sent as a matter of course and form to the Secretary of State, and therefore the ministers individually will not become cognizant of them, or have the curent knowledge of which I speak.
Now you get a despatch with reference, we will suppose, to the Pacific fisheries, and you send it off without consideration to the Secretary of State. What has this new department under the Secretary of State to do with it? The minister says it must be docketed, registered, an abstract made of it then it is to be sent-by whom? By the Secretary of State. Where? To the proper department. Is the Secretary of State a better judge of the department to which each despatch should be sent than would be the Prime Minister and the Council hearing the despatch and becoming cognizant of it? There does not seem to be much advantage gained in that respect. But there are despatches coming in which are confidential, which belong primarily to the Prime Minister alone, which sometimes never go beyond the purview of the Prime Minister, or may be one or two of his most responsible colleagues. What is to be done with those despatches? Are they to be bundled off to the Secretary of State, put into thei hands of his docketers, and abstracters and registered? Then what becomes of their confidential nature? Does not the Prime Minister see that neither he nor his Council can divest themselves of the necessity of looking at those despatches in the first instance, in order to separate, if nothing else, what are purely confidential and what are partly confidential, from those which are matters of course? But let that pass. Now that the Secretary of State has had them docketed, and bracketed and abstracted, he looks them over and says, I am of opinion that this goes to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or it goes to the Department of Agriculture, or it goes to the Minister of Justice-some matter of international law, or something of that kind ; and he takes it upon himself to decide. The mistake, if there be one, is the mistake of one man, the judgment being the judgment of one man ; in the other case, the judgment being the judgment of the Council, the mistake would be more rare in the occurrence. Can your Secretary 63

of State be at the office always? What happens? As in every other department, it happens that one or two men in the department are the men who will actually direct affairs, they will be the persons who will do the distribution, and who will consequently send these things on their way, rightly or wrongly.
But having got that far-and I am anxious just to carry it out and see where it ends-having got that far, what does the Secretary of State say? His boss man, with $5,000 a year, tells him: This is to go to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it is a very important matter with reference to the seal fisheries of the Pacific, and it must go to that minister. What does it go to the minister for? Does the Secretary of State say to the minister: Here is a very important despatch about the seal fisheries; I want you to give me all the information of your department with reference to that matter, get your men to work, give me the abstracts, send me the papers, I want them here as quickly as possible, the Governor General is in haste to have an answer. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries does-what? Puts himself into the hands of his officers, sets his clerks to work, gathers together all the information he can, bundles it up, and sends it over to the Secretary of State. But the Secretary of State knows no more about it than the man in the moon, comparatively speaking. He bundles it over to his $5,000 officers and their clerks. They are the men who are to write the despatch, says the Prime Minister. I do not believe they are the men who ought to write the despatch. It strikes me that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who knows the business from the foundation up, historically and otherwise, in whose department are all the facts as well as all the history, is the man who has to determine the policy and is the man who has to lay down the tenor of the despatch and submit it to his colleagues. Now it is proposed that he is not to do it. He is to send over the information and these experts in the Secretary of State's Department are to prepare the despatch in answer to the one that was received and lay it before your Privy Council. That is the programme, as I understand it. If that is the programme what must you have ? You must have a replica of every department of the government in the Department of the Secretary of State, men who are as able as the ministers of the departments are, men who are just as well up in their history as the ministers of the departments; consequently you are to have, if you are going to have an effective service, a very costly and numerous service. But even though you have that, a minister says I am the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I have studied my department, I know

its history and its circumstances and consequently I would feel as though I were the one who was to go to council with the kind of despatch which should go in answer to the despatch which had come. Now, I am simply to be told to send my material over to this new bureau, and if one of these gentlemen wants to know something that he does not know, tote over there, coach him up and tell him how things are, what rocks he has to avoid, and what clear water he has to take as he sails along in this despatch business. I believe that difficulties and practical difficulties will be encountered in that respect which I doubt if the right hon. gentleman has thoroughly weighed. The objection I have to this system is that it is not effective unless you make a most thorough, expensive and expert system, and have in the department some man who knows as much about every department in the government as does the responsible minister himself in reference to its history and circumstances. The despatch comes back from the Secretary of State but it is not gotten up by the Secretary of State. He comes and goes. He is here to-day and there to-morrow. It is the permanent man who will do it, it will be the bureau man who will do that. When that despatch comes before the Privy Council there sits the minister whose department is concerned The despatch is read, he has had no guiding hand in it and he may not have been consulted. He may say:	I do not think it is a proper reply
to be made; I do not think this bureau man has got the spirit of this matter. What is to be done? You cannot pass it against the minister. You will do what you might have done at first much better, it seems to me; that is, you will put it in the minister's hands, then as you will necessarily have to put it in the minister's hands in the last resort and let him take hold of it and give you the idea of the department. No outside bureaucrat can have the atmosphere of the department who has not been brought up to the work and who does not know the history of it. I think that will go without any contradiction at all. It is impossible to live in South Africa and have an appreciation of the air of Alberta or of Saskatchewan. You cannot do it, and no simple clerk, no extra well paid clerk in the bureau can have the atmosphere of the department such as that which clings to it for fifty years and is the product of the experience, history and the knowledge of its men during that time. When I came, a boy almost, into the Department of Marine and Fisheries,
I knew nothing of the department more than its name. Upon whom did I depend? At that moment I leaned strictly on one of the most capable deputy ministers we ever Mr. FOSTVU,
had. He had his faults, as every deputy . minister has. That was our late lamented friend, Mr. Wm. Smith. He had the whole history of the Department of Marine and Fisheries in his head. There was not a subject you could bring up in regard to which he could not at first give you his version and point to the material relating to it which carried out his version of it. You never can have your expert in this bureau with the head on him, with the atmosphere and with the amount of knowledge that the man brought up in the department for fifteen or thirty, or it may be, forty years has; and so that is why I think that this matter will not come to a good conclusion in the end. Yes, we want system. Everything that refers to the Department of Marine and Fisheries should be registered, docketed, bracketed in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries own department, to be at his right hand when he wants it for any purpose whatever. Everything that you want docketed in reference to this matter can be done by two expert men in the Privy Council, attached to the Prime Minister himself who can keep what is necesary to the Privy Council-a record of all the transactions under that head. That can be done by two or three good business-like, expert men in the office of the Privy Council as well. In this I am not opposing our extension; no one wants to do that. I am not saying that these matters are not multiplying, but if they are multiplying they are multiplying . by additions in each department, each taking its quota of added burden, but each department is well able to do this work and the Lord knows every one of them has a pay-roll big enough to do it. So, I repeat what I said at first. It seems that you add but another to the percolating media through whose hands this business would run, through which it would retrace itself until it came out at the same point at which it went in. You have a more simple, economical and thorough manner of dealing with this matter if you attach a little body of expert clerks to the Privy Council, put them under the Prime Minister, where, I think, these things ought to be and let them do all this work of keeping the records so that the Prime Minister and council, when they want to know the history of an affair, shall have the records and the abstracts under their own hand to show them what they need to know instead of having 'to hunt through the different departments to find this information. I just state these things because I want to see what we are going into before we go into it, and to see whether it will be a change for the better or not.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words upon this question before it goes through.

The record that is to be found in the library of parliament is rather interesting when contrasted with the proposal which is being made to the House to-day.
I remember very distinctly that years ago there was, from this side of the House, a strong attack made upon the Conservative government of the day because of the number of the departments we had in the Canadian government. The example of the United States was set before us of a country with something like 65,000,000 or 75,000,000 people running the government with only six departments, or seven at the outside, one of which was supposed to be an artificial department, while they said that in Canada we had to have eleven or twelve.
I remember Mr. John Charlton vigorously attacking the government for it, and I remember some hon. gentlemen who are today in the House doing the same thing and saying that for the size of the country we were entirely too extravagant, that we were burdened by too much government, that we were not economical, that we were spreading out and that we were making the government very much more expensive.
That debate occurred upon a proposal to establish the two controllerships of customs and inland revenue, which resembled, in one respect, under-secretaries of state in the imperial parliament. The controller-ships did not carry the full rights or salaries of ministers of the Crown. It was proposed that the controllers should be paid $4,000 each, but that proposal was denounced as unwarrantable extravagance, the country was told that the government were spending money at a most reckless and unjustifiable rate. The present government, however, had not been long in power before they raised the two controllerships to full-fledged departments wdth a minister of the Crown at the head of each, and with full departmental staffs, with highly paid offi cials. Then they established the Department of Trade and Commerce, which they claimed was justified because of the expansion of business in the country. It is now proposed to establish practically another department to be called the Department of the Exterior, to carry on correspondence with foreign countries and perhaps with the mother country relating to business that ought to be carried on through the various existing departments. It is only a year since we were told there was need for some one, who might be regarded as an expert, to look after this foreign correspondence, and Mr. Mackenzie was proposed by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself as a suitable person. Within a year the same right hon. gentleman informs the House that it is desired to create a new department to do that work. What is going to become of Mr. Mackenzie? This is the very work, as I understood, that he was to do. It was ne-63J	_	' .	1
cessary to have an expert and he was the man of experience who might be regarded as an expert. Has Mr. Mackenzie not fulfilled the requirements of the situation? All we have heard about him is that he has been fully equal to his task, in every respect. Is the Secretary of State so busy that he cannot attend to this work, that his department is overburdened ? I have always understood that it was an ornamental or supernumerary department, not having very much to do. Yet the Secretary of State is to have another staff under him to carry on this work. Before this government came into power they said that the ten or eleven departments then existing were too many, but to-day they have fourteen departments and one or two sub-departments, and they propose to create another, entailing increased expense which cannot be justified. The expense that they denounced a few years ago as entirely unjustifiable is now, thev say, absolutely necessary. If it is necessary to have a new department to carry on that correspondence, then the existing departments must be overworked. Are they? The country do not think they are. Some, I think, are overworked, but there are many others that are not, and it is generally understood that the Department of the Secretary of State is not one of those whieh are overworked.
Another grave objection to this proposal is that the heads of the existing departments will not be in a position to properly answer inquiries by members of this House in reference to their departments, because correspondence which should be conducted by the heads of the various departments will be conducted by the head of this new department. Thus, for instance, if we ask a question of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, he will say:	Oh, that information is not in my department, it is in the possession of the Department of the Exterior. The head of the new department will really have the right to lay down the policy of the other departments, to become the diplomat of the government. I understand it will be the duty of the head of the new department to prepare a reply to any communication from abroad and that that reply will be submitted to the Privy Council, without being submitted to the minister of the department concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It goes to the Privy Council.
And not to the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Then I cannot understand how any minister of a department can keep in touch with the line of policy in his department, for which he is responsible, if correspondence relating to it is to

be answered by some one else on lines suggested by that other person's judgment. I think it will result in confusion and will stultify the ministers in their administration. When a new minister enters a department he sometimes proposes changes in its policy; he may be more enterprising than his predecessor and lay down a distinct line of policy, the result of mature deliberation, as has been done by the Postmaster General in several lines, and by the Minister of Railways. My contention is that he cannot keep in proper touch with his department under the system now proposed and cannot be in a position to properly answer questions relating to his department that mav be put to him by members of this House. To summarize, the creation of the new department will give rise to confusion and prevent the existing departments from being as valuable as they are to-day. It will mean a new department, an increase of expense, a new staff of highly paid officials and will involve an acknowledgment that the departments that are to-day charged with the responsibility of that work are not equal to the task imposed upon them. I do not think that is very creditable to the government. It means discrediting the man the government got authority to appoint only a year ago to carry on the foreign correspondence, and keep in touch with it, and be prepared to give any department information as to any business that might come under his notice. Mr. Mackenzie's business is to be done away with and the Privy Council is to be shorn of a good deal of its important work. The clerk of the Privy Council and the assistant clerk were in the past supposed to be valuable men, but they will not be so in the future. Taken all in all, this is another evidence of the extravagance of the present government, of that expansion which a few years ago they declared was entirely unjustifiable. It is an evidence that there is something wanting when the affairs of this government cannot be carried on by fourteen departments and one or two supernumeraries, and they want to appoint another to help them to do it.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWOHTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose that on this occasion, in considering the resolution which has been proposed, the principle involved rather than any question of detail is the subject of discussion, though necessarily details must also be taken into account. Of the necessity for some step of this nature I am entirely satisfied. The necessity for it has been impressing itself upon my mind for more than two years past, and I think a consideration of one or two actual incidents of public business will convince any one that some such course must be taken if the business affairs of this country are to be carried on in proper or even in order- * Mr. SPROULE.
ly fashion. The relations which subsist between the Department of Justice, or the Minister of Justice of the day, and other departments or other ministers are very similar to those which subsist between an advising counsel or solicitor and his clients. Of necessity the Department of Justice is consulted about many matters of daily routine or of ordinary business in the different departments of the country's service, and on that account, in the disposition which is made of despatches such as has been outlined by the Prime Minister, it is very frequently the case that a despatch relating to some question of a legal character must necessarily go not only to the department which is acquainted with the facts of the matter to be dealt with, but also to the Department of Justice. For that reason it was not long after I had taken charge of the Department of Justice, two years and seven months ago, that different incidents connected with external affairs of Canada came to my knowledge, which impressed me with the feeling that there ought to be and must be some change made in the present manner of conducting business of that character, if our business was to be properly carried on. Let me mention one of the incidents to which I have alluded. Every one knows of the seizure some years ago of a Canadian ship by the government of Uruguay. The 'Agnes Donahue' was seized by that republic upon a charge of poaching within territorial waters, and the men on the vessel were imprisoned for some time. A special messenger, a legal gentleman of the province of Nova Scotia, from which province the ship's owners and the ship's crew in the main came, was sent specially by this government to South America in an effort to arrange the matter and secure some kind of settlement, with the result that the ship's crew were liberated. But the ship's owners have not to this day received any compensation for the seizure of their ship, and there is in consequence a claim for such compensation against the government of that republic being still promoted by the government of Great Britain urged thereto under representations from the government of Canada. Despatches in relation to that matter are continually passing through the British Foreign Office and Colonial Office to Canada. The matter involved is necessarily of legal character. These despatches very frequently, two years and a half ago, were being referred to the Department of Justice simultaneously with a like reference of the same despatches to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The Department of Marine and Fisheries, so to speak, was a client, and the Department of fustiee was its legal adviser. When endeavouring to take up the matter and get acquainted with the details, so as to be in

a position to advise upon it and deal with it, I found what I might without impropriety call an enormous file of correspondence and documents of one kind and another with reference to it already accumulated in the Department of Justice. After acquainting myself with the circumstances as well as I was able, I was in a position to frame some sort of recommendation or answer to the reference that had come to me from council. When that recommendation was brought up in council and discussed, I found that it did not altogether meet the views of my colleague in charge of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. A consultation took place between us in consequence, a consultation which, if it was necessary, might just as well have been had beforehand, and after we had come to an agreement in the matter, we thought we could unite upon a recommendation as to the course which ought to be taken. In the course of that consultation, I ascertained that there was a file of at least equal size in the Department of Marine and Fisheries on this subject, and some remark led to the discovery that in the Department of the Secretary of State there was a third portentous file, which in the course of the months had grown up about this affair. If these despatches seemed to be merely of a formal character, not calling for determination of any line of policy and not involving any question of doubt they might be referred simply to the State Department, and might be answered from that department as a matter of routine business, without going to any other department at all. The result was that in that matter, which after all was simply a good sized lawsuit, there were no few'er than three files in three departments each of which had to some extent been engaged with it. It struck me that was not business-like and that it ought to be changed. Since then I have been discussing this situation with my colleagues and in that spirit urging that some such steps as now proposed should be taken.
Let me mention just one other occurrence of entirely different character but which illustrates the imperfections of the present system. Emergencies arise; during the absence of the First Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at the Colonial Conference in 1907 there arose an occurrence of serious danger, I think I may say, out of the seizure of a ship in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. It was in midsummer; the only ministers here were the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself on the day that necessity for action took place. It was certainly a serious enough situation that faced us. Neither of us knew anything of similar occurrences which had taken place as we afterwards found out and which of course would be well known to the Minister
of Marine and Fisheries. There was necessity for prompt action; it was a situation involving a very great deal of anxiety at the time. Happily all went well, perhaps more by good fortune than by good management. I am thankful to say the situation never even came to the knowledge of the industrious newspaper reporter, and nobody knew anything about it. Now, if there had been a department of external affairs with a permanent secretary or staff acquainted with all business of a nature such as I have in mind, the difficulty which then was of most serious character would have been to a very large extent obviated. There would have been some one who would have known the current of affairs in connection with matters of that sort and who would have knowledge of precedents which would have been most useful to guide. In this case the only thing to be done was to get all the knowledge possible by personal application to different clerks in different departments and to go, as I did go, from department to department trying to find out things without letting anybody know why I wanted the information. It was a matter that I felt it was of utmost importance should not become public property, and the going from clerk to clerk in different departments to gather piecemeal bits of information without letting it be known what the difficulty was that had sprung up, was I believe not in the interest of the public business of the country. The matter directly involved foreign relations ; it directly involved circumstances which if there had not been friendly relations existing might very well enough have led in our dealings with other countries to an actual rupture of friendliness. Under these circumstances I became strongly impressed with the necessity of some such step as is now proposed. So far as I was able to follow the observations of the hon. member (Mr. Foster) I did not gather that he objects to the proposal in itself, but rather that he thinks the details of the scheme so far as outlined might be improved upon if a small staff of expert assistants were attached to the First Minister himself. I may say at once that so far as I am concerned that step would meet with my entire approval. That is however, the merest question of detail. The one important thing in the scheme now proposed is the permanent head who by this resolution is to be appointed with a salary of $5,000, the same as any other deputy. He will, of course, like any other deputy, be acting under the superintendence of some minister. That minister, whatever department he may have in charge, may be here to-day and gone to-morrow, and that may be so even though he be the First Minister. In that respect it is no difference whether the minister to whose department this deputy of external affairs is attached is the First

Minister or any of his colleagues. This work is analogous to work of the Department of State; and in other countries we have such duties discharged by the Secretary of State. It seemed not improper ; it seemed the best course to attach these duties to the Department of the Secretary of State. You will have then a gentleman appointed to be the permanent Under Secretary of State for External Affairs. As time goes on he will become saturated, I hope, with the atmosphere or the spirit of that department which the hon. gentleman so eloquently described. His usefulness will, of course, increase with time, and if we can secure, as I think we may very possibly be able to secure in the original appointee to that position if this measure becomes law, a gentleman of experience, expert, able in the discharge of just such duties, so much the better, because we shall have a good foundation laid whereupon to build. With such a permanent official appointed, he need not in the beginning at any rate be surrounded by an army of clerks. I should hope that two or three, or at most four or five efficient assistants in the way of clerks assigned to work under him, may be entirely sufficient for the carrying on of the business of this department. The additional expense to the country will simply be the $5,000 which the under secretary will receive together with the remuneration to be paid to any new clerks who may be required for the service of this Department of External Affairs.
It is very possible, I think, that, by assigning to these duties of this department some of the present clerks in the State Department, who, perhaps, could be spared, it will be unnecessary to call for the services of even the few additional clerks that I have referred to. But, once you get a department established of this character, you have that one man, the permanent under-secretary to whom I have referred, who is charged with responsibility for these things-he and his Minister the Secretary of State. Take one of the cases I have mentioned by way of illustration: A despatch comes with regard to which either the permanent under-secretary or the temporary minister in charge feels that he cannot make the answer to council without consulting somebody else. If it is a formal matter, if it is a matter he knows all about, and he feels that he does not need to go to any of his colleagues for purposes of consultation, he prepares his answer to council at once and that is an end of that transaction. But if it i3 a matter of more difficult character, if, for instance, it concerns the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the policy of that department, and also involves some question of international law,-what then should be done? Either that deputy has a personal conference, if he wants it, or Mr. AYLESWORTH.
communicates by correspondence, with the department interested, or the minister himself sees his colleague on the subject. The most harmonious relations, I am very glad to state, exist between the members of the government, and we can see each other with the utmost freedom, and with the utmost pleasure, at any time and discuss any matter of the country's business. It is not of necessity that there should be even the formality of the writing of letters; the ministers who are interested in the matter can meet, and in half-an-hour, or, perhaps in five minutes, settle upon the line of answer to be sent,-if not upon the wording, at all events upon the substance, of what is to be done with reference to this despatch. Instructions are given to the deputy head, who, probably with his own pen, will frame an answer, ne being in a . better position, from superior knowledge of the craftsmanship, to frame a despatch than even the minister himself. And, as a re suit, you get the best way of handling matters which otherwise are more or less complicated and might occasion difficulty and trouble. I do not apprehend, if this resolution is carried and the Bill to be founded upon it is passed, any continuation of the practical difficulties which I have already, myself, experienced on several occasions, and which in my mind have given rise to a feeling that! some step of thi3 character is absolutely necessary. There ought to be some one man at least who would have all the strings in his hands, would know what had passed before and would see to it that what was going out from this government was not inconsistent with what had gone before but was in continuation of the general line of policy which, in regard to dealing with any particular matter that may have come up, had already been adopted by the government.
What do you propose to do now with the officer who was assigned to that duty last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When we get into committee, I will answer that. Motion agreed to and House went into committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: It means that Canada must carry on some external relations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It means that Canada has to carry on external relations-
What has she been doing for the last forty years?	,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Not only for
the last eleven years but for the last forty years, and even before confederation,- every government must carry on such relations. But I believe that the time has come when there must be a department to carry on these relations, because the business cannot efficiently be done otherwise. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) asks: What about Mr. Mackenzie? Mr. Mackenzie will remain where he was placed last year. He is in the Department of the Privy Council, and his duty is to look after the foreign and imperial correspondence. He will have precisely the same duties to perform as he is performing at the present time.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us briefly what Mr. Mackenzie has been doing?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He looks after the imperial and foreign correspondence. When it is brought to him, he has to enter it in a book, docket it and distribute it. That is the duty of Mr. Mac kenzie.
He is attached now to the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He remains attached to the Privy Council. But the department we have now in mind is not only a clerical one, is not only to perform the clerical work which Mr. Mackenzie has to perform. My hon. friend understands very well what will bel the duties of this department: There is to be a permanent official the Under Secretary of State for external affairs, whose duty and business would be to keep posted from day to day on the external history of Canada as it progresses. Despatches comet relating, let us say, one to the Justice Department, one to the Marine and Fisheries, one to the Post Office, one to the Customs and one to the Interior. They are distributed to these departments, and there they are lost-that is, so far as the other departments are concerned; each minister has the despatch that has been sent to him but that is all. We want a department in which the history of all these despatches will be kept and followed from day to day.
Is Mr. Mackenzie not doing that? .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is doing that simply as a clerical department.

I wish to say to the Prime Minister that it would help us a great deal in arriving at a decision on this matter if we had statistics of the number of these despatches received daily, or monthly, and the necessity for the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a very fair question. I have not the statistics to-dajr, I will have them at the next stage of this Bill; I shall be happy to bring down, all the statistics the hon. gentleman has mentioned. Now, my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said a moment ago that when he came to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, being, as he said, a boy, and knowing nothing of the business of the department, he had to rely upon a very able man, Mr. Wm. Smith, and he paid him a very deserved compliment. But I may say to my hon. friendl that after the experience which he has acquired in thirty years of public life, and with all the attention he has given to it, were he again to return to-morrow to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, he would still largely have to rely upon his deputy minister. It is not expected of a minister that he should carry in his mind all the details of the office, which have to be gathered by the deputy minister. The time of the minister is too precious, he would not be able to do justice to his department if he were compelled to keep in mind all the details which properly come before the deputy minister. I may say to my hon. friend that he would need such a deputy minister as he had under him before. I may say to him that when I came into office, now twelve years ago, and when despatches began to come in relating to foreign affairs, I had not in the Department of the Privy Council any official who could inform me, or upon whom I could rely; I had to go to another officer, who is fortunately well qualified for that position, I have no hesitation in giving his

name, Mr. Pope, the under secretary-and get from him all the information I needed relating to those foreign affairs, before I could come to a decision and advise my colleagues, or His Excellency the Governor General, in relation thereto. It is therefore indispensable, I think, that at this time we should have what every other government has, a department of external affairs, where everything relating to our foreign relations may be found, and that instead of their being scattered as at present in the various departments, they should be concentrated in one department, where we can get them at a moment's notice, a department in charge of a man who is acquainted, not only with that department, but with the affairs of all the departments in so far as they relate to external affairs.
What are the statutory powers you are going to give to this new department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are found in this section:
The Secretary of State as head of the said department shall have the conduct of all official communications between the government of Canada and the government of any other country in connection with the external affairs of Canada, and shall be charged with such other duties as may be from time to time assigned to the said department by order cf the Governor in Council in relation to such external affairs, or to the conduct and management of international or intercolonial negotiations, so far as the same may appertain to the government of Canada.
These are large powers. Every confidential report will go to that department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will be in the discretion of the Governor in Council to say whether any confidential report shall go to the department or not; some may go there and others may not. But the hon. gentleman knows very well that there must be some department to which even confidential despatches may be assigned. The one thing I want to impress upon the committee is the necessity for the government of Canada to have now a department in which the information which is now scattered over all the departments, may be concentrated for the advantage of the ministers.

The right hon. gentleman spoke of a committee of external affairs as a necessity of government. The history of this country during the past forty-two years will show that his words could not be taken in their literal acceptation. If the right hon. gentleman meant that some official activity, some departmental work in connection with external affairs, is a necessity of this government, then we Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
would all be inclined to agree with him. Now, I do not find any fault with the object which is aimed at by this legislation, I am not disposed to quarrel with that. The right hon. gentleman said that the object of the creation of this new department was three-fold:	First, the allotment of despatches; secondly, the creation of a history of each subject to which reference can be made from time to time; and thirdly, the preparation of a draft despatch in reply to any communication from abroad. Those were the three objects, and I regard them as very desirable and necessary objects. But I have yet to see that it is necessary to create a new department for that purpose. Let me point out to the right hon. gentleman what he is doing. In the United States at the present time there are nine departments. One of these is the Department of the Secretary of State, which deals with all foreign relations; and one would think that if the Department of the Secretary of State in the United States can deal with, and tabulate, and prepare the history of these matters connected with the foreign relations of a population of nearly 100,000,000, the Department of the Secretary of State in Canada could do the same thing for our foreign relations, which are very limited indeed as compared with those of the United States. If in the Commonwealth of Australia, where they have only eight departments, and where the Minister of External Affairs is the Prime Minister of the commonwealth, they can get along without a Secretary of State, it does seem to me a piece of unnecessary machinery in this country to have, not only a Department of Secretary of State, but a new Department of External Affairs as well. In other words, to carry on the machinery of government in this respect for the people of Canada, requires not only the machinery which is sufficient for ninety millions of people in the United States, but also the machinery that carries on the same governmental work for the government of Australia. I was much struck with the history of affairs given by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, but I would not be disposed to draw from his remarks exactly the same conclusion which he did, although he did not very much dispute the argument which was put forward by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). The difficulty in the whole matter has been that you have, not too little, but too much machinery. You have three departments getting in each others way, the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Justice, in the illustration which was given to us by the Minister of Justice. What you want is not more machinery, but better organization. You have any amount of machinery now. My hon.

friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) referred to the fourteen departments of government He was altogether too modest. There are more than fourteen departments. Can the Secretary of State tell me how many departments of government there are now?
There are fourteen departments of government.
Seventeen.
For example, there is a Department of the Interior and a Department of Indian Affairs.
Both under one minister.

The hon. gentleman is speaking of ministers. I was speaking of departments, and my hon. friend from Grey was referring to departments. I say there are a great many more than fourteen departments. After all, the creation of something that you call ia Department of External Affairs will amount to nothing. It is the organization which you must create for the purpose of coping with this work that will count in the end. I am absolutely unconvinced by anything in the argument put forward by the Prime Minister and by the Secretary of State that the mere creation of this department is going to advance you one single step. Take, for instance, the illustration put very cogently by the Minister of Justice this afternoon:	What should have
been done with the case of the ' Agnes DonoghueP' What, in the name of common sense, had the Department of Marine and Fisheries to do with it? Can any human being conceive why the Department of Marine and Fisheries should have interfered with that? Suppose a British subject went to some other country and undertook to enter into a railway enterprise there, suppose that he obtained a charter for a railway and that the government there confiscated his undertaking in a manner unwarranted by international law and complaint was made to this government; would the complaint go to the Department of Railways and Canals for Canada? You might just as seriously send that to the Department of Railways and Canals as to send this particular complaint to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It should have gone to the Secretary of State and some minister whether before or after the creation of this department, must, in a case of that kind, invoke the aid of the Department of Justice. The creation of this new Department of External Affairs does not advance the work of government in this respect one jot or iota as far as I can understand.
I do not for one moment lift my voice against the expenditure of $5,000, or a larger sum of money, for doing the very necessary work that ought to be done in connection with our administration, as far as foreign affairs are concerned, but I do protest against the unnecessary multiplication of the departments of the government. What will it amount to? You create this department, that department, and the other department, and then you create this branch, that branch, and the other branch, when, as the returns brought down this very session indicate to this House and the country, you do not even go to the trouble to indicate to the clerks of these departments wh'at their duties are. Return after return has been brought down and laid upon the table of this House indicating that nearly every department of this government has, up to the present time, absolutely failed to comply in any sense with the legislation of this parliament passed in July last. The creation of departments amounts to nothing, and the creation of branches of departments amounts to nothing, but the creation of a live system of organization in any department of the government does count for something and that is after all what the Prime Minister himself must desire in this matter.
There is one other circumstance to which I would like to invite attention, and which to me has seemed important in view of what has been suggested to me this afternoon by hon. gentlemen who have been members of an administration, a privilege which, to the present time, it has not been my fortune to enjoy. In the Commonwealth of Australia, situated, in so far as Great Britain is concerned, very much as we are, the Minister of External Affairs is the Prime Minister; so that all the matters of a confidential character alluded to this afternoon, some of which possibly could not be disclosed even to the Cabinet as a whole, shall come to the Prime Minister as Minister of External Affairs, and he shall use his judgment and discretion as to how far they must be kept confidential even as far as members of his cabinet are concerned. If we are to concede what the Prime Minister has argued for-and I am not disposed to concede it because I am not yet convinced-but if one were disposed to concede the argument of the Prime Minister that a new department is necessary for the mere purpose of organization, then I say that that department should be under the control of the Prime Minister and not under the control of the Secretary of State. Mr. Chairman, that is the way the situation strikes me at the present time. Let me just add in conclusion that I do not see that any of the dangers or difficulties which were pointed out by the Minister of Justice this afternoon would be in the least obviated by the creation of this new department. The minister at the head of the Department of External Affairs might be away, the minister in charge of any one of the departments might be away and still an emergency might arise. You may always expect contingencies of any kind in matters of government. The creation of this department

will not do away with them.
