I thoroughly concede, of course, what the Minister of Justice argued, that the creation of a history of each of these subjects touching external affairs under the control of a capable officer would be of infinite importance to the ministers who are here in Ottawa and who have to deal with situations of that kind, but I do not see that it is very much forwarded by the mere creation of this department and by calling it a Department of External Affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that after all the difference between the two sides of the House on this question is not very great. It seems to be very minute indeed. If I understand the criticisms that have been offered by hon. gentlemen opposite, they have admitted frankly the necessity and advisability of having special officers detailed for the work that we have in mind. They say that it would be sufficient to increase the personnel of the department of the Privy Council over which the Prime Minister presides. The Prime Minister may not necessarily be the President of the Council. Sir Charles Tupper, when he came into office, took the portfolio of Secretary of State. When Sir John Macdonald formed his government in 1878 he took the portfolio of the Interior in addition to his duties of Prime Minister. When the present government was formed in 1896 I came to the conclusion that the Prime Minister should be President of the Council. I am still of that opinion. Very shortly after I took office I discussed this point with Sir Charles Tupper and he thought I should have taken the portfolio of Secretary of State. I differed with him; I thought the Prime Minister should be President of the Council. Whenever there is a change of government my hon. friend on the other side of the House may not become President of the Council but he may become Secretary of State, or take another portfolio. It does not matter under which minister the Department of External Affairs may be placed, it is sufficient that it should be under a responsible minister. The fact that there will be some confidential despatches which the Prime Minister may have to keep to himself does not weigh very much with me; in fact, in the course of my experience during the last twelve years, there never came to me a despatch which I thought I could not take to council. On the contrary, upon every occasion that any matter of this kind occurred, I have always thought it preferable to take the whole cabinet into the confidence of the Prime Minister and of His Excellency the Governor General.
That would be on your judgment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course. I do not believe there is anything which should be kept from council, although there might be some things that it would possibly be advisable to keep within the Prime Minister and the Governor General and perhaps one or two of the colleagues of the Prime Minister for the time being. But this matter will not be changed when there is a Department of External Affairs. One thing that I would like to impress upon hon. gentlemen opposite is that the present system cannot continue any longer. It is very true that for the forty years that confederation has lasted we have not had such a department, but forty years ago the foreign relations of the government were not the same as they are to-day. Canada has increased very much during that time, and, in my humble judgment, we have come to the point when we must pay much more attention to these matters than we ha ve in the past. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), who has been in the government, thought it should be sufficient if we were to increase the number of clerks and detail three or four of them to give us the information which we want to have. I do not dispute that this is a method which might perhaps work. It may be that it would be sufficient to detail a staff in the Department of the Privy Council or the Secretary of State and assign to them the work we now have in mind. I do not think there can be any discussion as to the necessity of doing this work. It must be done, and it must be organized promptly. But we have thought after consideration that it was better to give to this branch the dignity and importance of a department by itself, as is done in other countries.
Dignity is very costly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I do not think my hon. friend can say that with any truth. We will have a deputy head, perhaps two or three officers and no more. When we come to another stage in the discussion of this Bill, we will place before the House exactly the staff they want to have and for which we will ask the sanction of parliament.
Could the minister now tell us how many will be required and their salaries?

It is believed that not more than four will be required in any event and three may be sufficient. It is further believed that gentlemen now in the service may be transferred to this new department at the salaries which they are now receiving.

I have been looking up the record to see what was said at the time of Mr. Mackenzie's appointment. I find the Prime Minister said that Mr. Mackenzie had been appointed a clerk in the office

of the Privy Council and that his duties would be to classify and keep track of the correspondence which was accumulating very fast from the imperial authorities and colonial and foreign governments. He was to collate it and I thought answer it as well, and I think the Prime Minister spoke of Mr. Mackenzie's familiarity with newspaper work and his educational endowments. Is Mr. Mackenzie to be at the head of the new department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. McKenzie will remain in the office of the Privy Council and this new department will be under the control of the Secretary of State. It is not contemplated that Mr. Mackenzie will be at the head of the new department.
If Mr. Mackenzie is to remain in the Privy Council and collate this correspondence, what is the necessity of this department ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the despatches were to be sent directly to the Department of External Affairs, Mr. Mackenzie would perhaps be transferred to that department; but it is thought better that the despatches as they come from the Governor General should be sent to the Privy Council because the ministers then can have a friendly discussion over it. Some of these despatches are not of importance, but others are of great importance and it is thought better that they should come directly to the Privy Council before going to the Exterior Department. Mr. Mackenzie will continue to look after the correspondence as he does to-day.

If a communication should come from the British Ambassador at Washington it would be received by the Governor General; the Governor General would send it to tlje Privy Council, the Privy Council would hand it over to Mr. Mackenzie, Mr. Mackenzie would send it to the Department of the Exterior and the new department would collate it again, register it and I presume answer it on their own judgment and responsibility, because up to this time the information given us is that the Privy Council would expend no inquiry or intelligence on it, but after the answer would be prepared the Privy Council would decide whether it was an appropriate answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is about right. The communication will go to His Excellency and be referred by him to the Privy Council; the Privy Council will send it to the Department of External Affairs with instructions or without instructions and the Department of External Affairs, when they have passed on it and prepared an answer, will send it back to council to be discussed.
Council will then discuss it, sign it, and send it back through the same channel, I presume. It will make a much slower mode of carrying on business.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no.

Referring to the number of departments, we have the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Labour, the Customs Department, and now the Department of the Exterior, the Department of Marine, with the sub-department of Fisheries; the Department of the Interior, the Department of Indian Affairs, the Department of Finance, the Department of Inland Revenue, the Post Office Department, the Department of the Privy Council, the Department of Public Works, the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Justice and of the Solicitor General, the Department of Railways and Canals, and the Department of Mines. In all we have twenty-one departments and yet this government condemned their predecessors for having eleven departments. I am told the Printing Bureau is now to be a new department.
As to the working of this new department, supposing a communication comes from the British Ambassador referring to the Fisheries Treaty, would that communication be submitted to the Department of Marine and Fisheries before being dealt with by the Department of the Exterior ? Where will that department get the information required to answer ft ? Would it be answered before going to the Department of Marine and Fisheries ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That depends upon the circumstances. If a despatch came from Mr. Bryce to the Governor General on a question of the fisheries, it would be sent to the Privy Council, and the Privy Council would send it to the Department of External Affairs.
What is Mr. Mackenzie doing in the meantime?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is an officer of the Privy Council, and looks after the work assigned to him.
What is that special work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The important correspondence of the Privy Council. The Department of External Affairs may perhaps be able to give an answer in five minutes, or it may have to get information from the Department of Marine or some other department. But when a question has been the subject of communication from day to day or week to week for some time, the Department of External Affairs would probably be able to answer it on the spot without reference to any other department.

I have listened most attentively to the Prime Minister's explanation and to the explanation given by the Secretary of State. When the Secretary of State was asked how many departments there were, it was really a study to view his countenance. Of course, he is a young minister. When he has been there for a year, he will probably be able to count the number of departments there are in this government; but it will be a business for him just the same. The Secretary of State was very practical when my hon. friend from East Grey asked about the officials already appointed. He answered that the probability was that there would be transfers of three or four from other departments and that there would be really no more new officers outside of the under secretary. .That of course went back directly to Mr. Mackenzie. A year ago Mr. Mackenzie was picked out of the fourth estate and appointed to this office, an office which was specially defined, the need of which was great, and a definition of the duties of that office was made by the Prime Minister. The difficulty was that things were not in order, the despatches were not classified and tabulated, and Mr. Mackenzie was put there to bring order out of disorder. Now, we are going to have the organization put in charge of the Secretary of State, and it seems to me that it was the idea of the Secretary of State that Mr. Mackenzie should go to his department and do his organizing and tabulating in that department. The Prime Minister says no, he is to be kept in the office of the Privy Council, and if his duties there are to be to tabulate and'keep a history of the documents, are you going to have two tabulations and two histories? That will not make matters more workable, but will make them more cumbersome; in fact, you will have just one more circumlocution office. I want to tell the Prime Minister, and it may be taken for what it is worth, as a minister who had something to do with such matters, that he will find that it is absolutely impracticable to have great questions, affecting intimately one department or another,_ adjusted without the active cooperation of the minister of the department. Mere matters of form an ordinary clerk can attend to; but our external affairs are now very important affairs. The Minister of Justice fairly made my hair stand on my head when he was depicting the heart-curdling vision-which he brought to the edge of the platform and then refused to raise the curtain upon- of war, bloody war which was on the very verge. What neighbour was it-Japan, China or the United States. Happily the Minister of Justice was here, and, without a single man of the fourth estate knowing anything about it, he settled the whole difficulty. Does this not show the Prime Minister how important our external affairs are? They are so Sir WILFRID LAURIEE.
important that they ought not to be in the hands of a second-rate or third-rate minister. I do not make any invidious distinctions. The young man who comes in as a new minister has yet to leam his business. As a rule the Department of the Secretary of State will go to a young man. He has not the drill, the experience, the wisdom necessary for our external affairs, which are important and are going to be more so, and upon their proper adjudication, with temper, delicacy of touch, wisdom and discernment, will depend whether there will be international disagreements or international peace. The best drill that I ever had since I came into public life was the drill I got in the Department of Marine and Fisheries when the Atlantic and Pacific fisheries questions were up. I would have been very sorry to have been deprived of having had that experience and the breadth and growth that it gave me. I was the right person to have that business in charge, because I was the head of that department. When I went there I relied upon my deputy minister, but I did not rely upon him entirely. I made every part of the department, which was a tremendously extended one, a special study, and within two years I knew the history and operation of every part of the department. Sir John Macdonald said: You are the minister of that department, and it is you who must take this matter in charge. I did so, with the assistance of the Governor General and the Minister of Justice, and it was the best drill I ever had, and was an antidote to the sickening mass of detail and party patronage business which every minister in the course of time gets so heartily sick of. You are going to take that from every department, you are going to have a bureau which will do that business. The Minister of Justice said that the officials would get saturated with the business in time; but you cannot sit in the Secretary of State's Department and know what the Minister of Agriculture or what the Minister of Marine knows about his own department. You will never do in that department what will be satisfactory to a responsible live minister unless he has a hand in the pie, and he has a right to have a hand there. You may bring from that bureau all that your new fledged diplomats may pen on paper but the minister whose department is chiefly affected will say: I do not agree with some parts of it, I will have to think it over; and then your merry-go-round starts again. I lay these difficulties before the Prime Minister and the thinking men of the House, so that they may be considered.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Bill (No. 90) to create a Department of External Affairs.-Hon. Charles Murphy- introduced and read the first time.
When dees the Minister of Agriculture propose to go on with the Civil Service Bill? I do not want to hurry him, but we will be getting into other business! now and that Bill should be considered.

The delay has been caused by the necessity of making out the schedules which we agreed to attach to the Bill. All the schedules are ready except those of the Senate and the House of Commons, and I cannot proceed with the Bill until the classification of the Senate and House of Commons employees is prepared. I am pressing it forward with all my power.
Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of Interior) moved second reading of Bill (No. 17) respecting immigration.
This requires some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This Bill differs in detail rather than in principle from the law passed some three years ago, and the necessity for the changes in detail arises from the changed conditions of immigration. The law now on the statute-book was the first action by parliament on the policy of selected immigration and since then circumstances have arisen which make it necessary to follow a policy of more and more restriction or more and more careful selection. This brings with it the difficulty of enforcing the law as it is, and we find that the law requires amending in order to make it more satisfactory in enforcement when tested by opposition which brings it under review of the courts. It is with the view of carrying out the principles contained in the existing Act and to make it more effective that this Bill has been framed. There is a provision against what is called assisted immigration. It has never been the policy of the government to assist immigration but there were no definite proceedings taken to actually prevent assisted immigration until an order in council was passed a year ago and that order in council is incorporated in the present Bill.
Do I understand that under this Bill there shall be no assisted immigration, either to steamships or to individual agents?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Bill is in accordance with the order in council at present existing, which provides for the exclusion from Canada of immigrants assisted by charitable organizations unless the immigrant has been approved by the authorized agent of the Canadian government before sailing.
I think that does not do away with the assistance to immigration if I understand it correctly, it relates only to the assistance given by a philanthropic or charitable institution.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

You will not accept the immigrants, notwithstanding the assistance given them, unless they are regarded as suitable when examined. But the question I asked is:	Do the government intend by this Bill to stop immigration that is assisted, for instance, by paying commission to those working in the United States to bring immigrants to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that I understand quite what my hon. friend wants to arrive at.

Take, for instance, the North Atlantic Trading Co., they got a lot of money that was really assistance to immigration, being paid a certain commission. The steamships also are paid a commission and so are agents operating in the United States. That I would call, in the ordinary acceptation of the term, assisted immigration. What I ask is: Do the government intend to stop this assistance or carry it out as heretofore?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) is hardly well advised in using the term * assisted immigration ' in referring to the matter mentioned. I should consider this immigration effort and not assistance to immigration. This Bill embodies the principle which is now contained in an order in council and which has always been the policy of this government in regard to immigration that there should be no assistance to immigrants to enable them to immigrate.
But, if you give them a reduced passage, would not that be assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The government has not
given anybody a passage of any kind at any price.

This Bill is a very considerable change from the provisions of the law which hitherto have governed our immigration system, and I have no hesitation in saying that it is a step forward upon the lines which have very often been advocated in this House, and more particularly on this side of the House. As I understand the measure, it does not in any way interfere with the system of favouring immigration which has existed hitherto; it does not disturb in any manner our immigration agencies established in the United States, in the British Isles and on the continent. It in no way changes the system of bonusing immigrants which has hitherto existed, and in

relation to which we are still governed by the order in council which has considerably enlarged the system, extending it to railway navvies and other classes, which, up to the time of passing that order in council, never had been comprised within the bonus system. What the Bill aims at particularly is to provide for a strict examination of immigrants when they land in Canada. It has been found-there is no doubt whatever about it-that our system of examination was utterly deficient. And the object of this legislation is to provide a system that will assure a more careful examination of incoming immigrants. I say that, so far as that goes, this law is a step forward. But the question which suggests itself, I am sure, to every member of this House who has taken any interest in the question of immigration is this: If this is a good law, if it provides a safeguard, against a class of immigrants who are not desirable in this country, whv has it not been enacted sooner? While giving credit to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) for this measure, I say it is fit and proper for us to ask why this safeguard was not provided ten or twelve years ago when we began receiving in this country such large quantities of immigration, when from an expenditure of about $100,000 a year or $125,000 a year, which was our limit up to 1896, we went up to an expenditure of $700,000, $800,000, and finally, even more than $1,000,000. As a consequence of a very much more expensive propaganda and the establishment of far more numerous agencies and of a system of bonusing which had never been known before, we have had an immense influx of immigrants. The conditions prescribed by this Bill were known to be necessary at that time. They were urged on this side of the House repeatedly when that wave of immigration began to invade Canada. This measure is taken largely from the American immigration regulations and law. Why did not we adopt it before? That is the serious observation I wish to lay before the minister-let him tell us why we are, so to speak, locking the stable door after the horse is gone? For that is what we are doing. The explanation must certainly be found in the fact that, during a certain number of years which former members of this House will certainly remember, we had given to the tendency of immigration to this country a push forward which was extremely imprudent. Not to go too extensively into affairs of the past, it will be remembered that, through the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company largely, the country paid out, speaking off-hand, but I think pretty closely to the figures-over $450,000 in bonuses and expenses of advertising. It will hardly be denied that in this we were doing an extremely imprudent Mr. MONK.
thing, for we never were able to find out what became of that money and to whom it was paid. I do not wish to go at too great a length into that phase of the question, and to recall a past which most of those who took an interest in the question at that time, I am sure, have still in mind. This proposed legislation, to my mind, shows the usefulness of the campaign, in this House and outside of this House, which was kept up by the opposition for a long time in order to secure the very provisions that we find in this Bill. And it is extremely regretable, I am sure, not only in the interests of our country, but in the interests of the immigrants of the better class who have come here and succeeded, that these enactments were not put into law before the large influx of immigrants into Canada, amounting, I suppose, in the last ten years, to over 800,000 people, had begun.
Let me say a word with regard to one of the dispositions of the Bill, and which is continued, if I may say so, in the principle of the Bill. The whole Bill proceeds upon what is to my mind a bad principle, and I venture to say that before long we will come to the conclusion in this House and in the country that that principle is not well founded. The whole Bill is founded on the principle of the examination of the immigrant after he lands, or is about to land, in Canada. I think that experience has demonstrated, and statistics will show, that this is a wrong principle. We should make sure that the immigrant is a fit and proper person to come to this country before he leaves the port of embarkation. This is what happens in practice: The immigrant will go to the booking agent, we will say, in the British Isles or on the continent. The agent is anxious in the first place to bring this immigrant within the bonus class, and I submit to my hon. friend the minister that with the wide order in council authorizing the payment of bonuses, it is not a very difficult task for an experienced booking agent to get that immigrant into the class which earns him a bonus. No examination whatever as to the physical condition of the immigrant takes place before landing. There is no inquiry whatever as to his moral qualifications to become a citizen of this Dominion. All that takes place is that the booking agent makes sure that he will earn, through this immigrant, his. bonus, and sells him a ticket. Everything induces the agent to direct this immigrant to Canada, if possible, not only because of the bonus he receives, but because of the generous commission he gets from the transportation company.
The immigrant arrives in Quebec, we will say. Now members of this House who have followed the proceedings of the Immigration Committee in the past sessions, know what

kind of an examination the immigrant undergoes there. It is exceedingly brief.- I think it was Mr. Scott, the superintendent, who told us that the examination is a matter of two or three minutes, or perhaps four minutes. The immigrant passes before a medical examiner at the port of arrival. There are a thousand or two thousand immigrants to be examined, and a train is waiting to carry them on to their destination. He will look at their eyes, at their external appearance, but no proper medical examination takes place. And I ask the House how is it possible in the short space allowed to the examiner, to make sure, even in the most superficial manner, of the qualifications of the immigrant to enter this country. He passes before a second officer and is immediately hastened on board the train, and moves away. Now what happens ? He arrives in Montreal or Toronto. The man we will suppose, is undesirable; we will suppose that he is guilty of some offence. He is immediately brought before one of our criminal courts, either for some worse or some petty offence. The magistrate asks him where he comes from, what steamship line brought him across. He is remanded, and through the immigration agent, as I understand, the department of my hon. friend the minister is communicated with. The department sends an officer to make sure of the fact. Deportation in that case is found necessary; the man is at our expense detained in jail, he is afterwards forwarded with a guardian at the expense of the country, as a rule, to the port where he landed, for instance at Quebec. When the steamer is out in the stream ready to go, he is taken on board the vessel and sent home. He arrives in Liverpool. They don't want him there, and will not receive him. He is sent on perhaps to London, and there what is the condition of that man ? It may be that he is only in the early stage of criminality, but he is an absolutely lost individual, utterly discouraged, ostracized, and his fate is one, although he may be a criminal, very much to be deplored.
In the case of those who are deported because they are afflicted with disease, which very often happens-we had last year over 800 deported after admission to this country-the case is infinitely more pitiful. The man is returned to the company that has brought him over, and he is sent back. If
he is the father of a family who came out here to prospect and found an establishment, he returns to his home in Europe, having expended all the money he had when he came out here to establish a home. He is absolutely discouraged, and becomes a very active agent in doing as much harm as possible to this country, spreading everywhere the idea that this is the very worst country a man could come to. Very often families are separated, and the utmost distress and grief accompany this deportation. Cases have come under my observation where the hardship is very great indeed. I have known of other cases of people deported from Montreal who, after having done a great deal of harm in that city, in a variety of ways which it is not necessary to dilate upon now, have been sent back to their own country. There was a case came under my own personal knowledge of a prostitute who arrived in this country from Europe. There was nothing apparently to prevent her admission to this country. She came to Montreal and established a house there, and after a time was brought before the magistrate, and had to be deported. It is evident that it was impossible at the port of entry to discover the objection that existed in that case, and a great deal of harm resulted. There is no doubt whatever that if inquiries had been made, and if that person had been told on the other side that it was absolutely useless for her to attempt to enter Canada, we would have been spared the expense and the disagreeable consequences which resulted in that case.
I have a few more remarks to make on this subject, but as we have now passed the hour of six o'clock I move that the debate be adjourned.
Motion agreed to.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
Would the Prime Minister be good enough to tell us what business will be taken up to-morrow?
